query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: An integrated computational method that combines DFT, Boltzmann transport, and ML-trained Green–Kubo simulations can accurately decouple and predict separate lattice and electronic thermal conductivities in HfNbTaTiZr, outperforming previous defect‐free bulk models.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy synthesized as a single-phase, solid solution with minimal defects and controlled oxygen content (ideally <1 wt.%).
generation.intervention: Apply the integrated computational approach: perform DFT to obtain electronic states and local lattice distortions; use Boltzmann transport theory to predict electronic conductivity; employ ML-trained Green–Kubo simulations to capture anharmonic lattice dynamics and compute lattice thermal conductivity.
generation.conditions: Analysis conducted over a temperature range from approximately 200 K to 1200 K on samples with high chemical homogeneity and well-controlled impurity content.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions and the variation of interatomic force constants inherent to the HEA structure.
generation.mechanism: Atomic-scale lattice distortions induce enhanced phonon scattering which decouples the lattice thermal conductivity from the electronic thermal conductivity. DFT-derived electronic states combined with Boltzmann transport capture the evolution of electron dynamics, while ML-trained Green–Kubo simulations effectively capture temperature-dependent anharmonic phonon transport.
generation.predicted_outcome: The method will predict lattice and electronic contributions to the overall thermal conductivity with an expected improvement (approximately 20–30% reduction in predictive error compared to earlier approaches) and quantitatively forecast a crossover regime where lattice transport predominates near 200 K and becomes comparable to the electronic contribution at higher temperatures.
generation.baseline: Existing defect‐free bulk models and analytical approaches that do not decouple lattice and electronic contributions, leading to conflated and less accurate thermal conductivity predictions.
generation.boundary: The approach is applicable to defect-poor HfNbTaTiZr samples within the temperature range of 200 K to 1200 K. Its accuracy may diminish for samples with significant impurity or defect concentrations, or outside this temperature range.
generation.uncertainty: While a 20–30% improvement in matching experimental results is anticipated, precise quantitative gains are uncertain due to limited experimental datasets and intrinsic complexities in decoupling overlapping electron-phonon contributions.

falsification_experiment.design: Compute the lattice and electronic thermal conductivities of HfNbTaTiZr at several discrete temperatures (e.g., 200 K, 400 K, 800 K, and 1200 K) using the integrated simulation approach. Independently prepare high-purity, low-oxygen HfNbTaTiZr samples and measure the total, lattice (via techniques like time-domain thermal reflectance), and electronic (via Hall measurements or terahertz spectroscopy) thermal conductivities.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the separate contributions predicted by the integrated approach deviate by more than 30% from the experimental data across the target temperature range, or if the predicted crossover in dominant heat transport near 200 K is not observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractLattice distortions are intrinsic features of all solid solution alloys associated with varying atomic radii; this phenomenon facilitates the formation of single-phase solid solutions. Using high-entropy alloys (HEAs), as an example, we investigate the influence of variations in inter-atomic separations for stabilizing and controlling their structural, mechanical, and thermodynamic properties. This is done through a combination of statistical mechanics analysis and molecular dynamics simulations on simplified 2D systems, as well as a 3D crystals with harmonic and anharmonic inter-atomic bonds with varying natural inter-atomic separations. Figure 3 shows the temperature dependence of the measured κ, and the derived values of κe and κg for NiCoFeCrMn and NiCoFeCrPd. One distinct feature of the concentrated alloys, relative to pure metals, is that in a pure metal the total thermal conductivity is dominated by κe, and κg is usually negligible. However, in concentrated alloys, κg seems to dominate at low temperatures and is comparable with κe at about room temperature. Chemical disorder appears to scatter electrons more effectively than phonons. In addition, in pure metals κ starts decreasing at a few tens of K, while in concentrated alloys κ keeps increasing up to at least 300 K (see Table 3). One major reason is that, due to the large and nearly constant resistivity of these complex alloys, κe almost linearly increases with temperature up to 300 K, which is very different from the behavior in pure metals. The theoretical description of the temperature dependence of κg for disordered alloys has been challenging. Recently, PbSnTeSe has been experimentally investigated by Fan et al. [] and Raphel et al. [,], who report appreciably similar results for the thermoelectric performance of the material (see below). The modelling of HEAs transport properties constitute a challenge, and both the simulation methods and their derived predictions have to be confronted to experimental data to assess their validity. In this context, we present in this paper for the first time a complete approach that allows one to obtain all the transport coefficients, including the figure of merit, of a high-entropy alloy. The thermoelectric transport properties of the PbSnTeSe high-entropy alloy have been calculated by combining state-of-the-art methods based on the special quasi-random structures approach to generate the HEA structure, the first-principles density-functional theory (DFT), and the Boltzmann transport and Green–Kubo theories. First, from the DFT-computed material electronic states, the electronic transport properties (electronic conductivity, Seebeck coefficient and electronic thermal conductivity) were calculated using the linearized Boltzmann transport equation, and the power factor was obtained. reading.lever: Integrate DFT, Boltzmann transport, and ML-trained Green–Kubo simulations to decouple lattice and electronic conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr.
reading.why: This combined computational approach, proven on PbSnTeSe, directly addresses the need to separate transport contributions and overcome limitations of previous defect‐free bulk models in refractory HEAs.
